                                 PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
                               SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

 JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                        §   BEFORE THE
 ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY                         §
 LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION                         §
 SERVICE CORPORATION TO                            §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF                       §
 CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY                         §   OF TEXAS
 FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST                          §
 SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION
 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE
 PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,
 CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,
 LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH,
 MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN
 SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,
 AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES


       REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION OF LAMPASAS
 J11 LANDOWNERS

        NOW COME Lampasas J11 Landowners (“Lampasas J11”), in the above-entitled and

 numbered cause and files these, its Replies to PUC Staff’s and J27, J25, J4 Opposition

 Landowner’s (“J27 Landowners”) Exceptions to the ALJs’ PFD which was issued August 20,

 2026, and in support thereof, would respectfully show as follows:


       PUC Staff and J27 Landowners support Route 487, But It Does Not Adequately

Reflect Environmental Integrity as There are Many Alternatives, including Route 894,

Which Avoid the Devastating Environmental Impact of a New Colorado River Crossing in

A Pristine Area on Link J11.




                                               1
         PUC Staff, joined by only one intervenor, continues to support Route 487. 1 The

Applicants recommended Route 894 as the best meets route in comparison with other

alternatives, as it was the most compliant with Commission rules and policies regarding routing.

Applicant witness Casey Petty testified as to some of the reasons why:


                 “Specifically, this route, as compared to the other filed alternative routes included

                 in the Application:


                 •         is approximately 223.7 miles in length, which is 9.7 miles longer than the

                 shortest filed route and approximately 20.7 miles shorter than the longest filed

                 route;


                 •         has an estimated transmission line cost of $1,680,919,000, which is

                 approximately 2.73% more than the least costly filed route and 9.52% less than

                 the most costly filed route; and


                 •         has 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of its centerline, which is five

                 more than the filed routes with the fewest habitable structures within 500 feet of

                 their centerlines and 99 less than the filed routes with the most habitable

                 structures within 500 feet of their centerlines.


                 My routing memorandum, Exhibit CDP-6, lays out additional factors I considered

                 in selecting Route 894. In addition, Route 894, like the other filed routes, was

                 judged to be feasible from an engineering perspective based on currently known




1 Staff Exceptions at 13

                                                     2
                    conditions, without the benefit of on-the-ground and subsurface surveys, as

                   further discussed in the direct testimony of Ms. Cooley. “ 2


          On cross-examination by Lampasas J11 Landowners, Oncor witness Marusak also

testified that the Applicants carefully studied all potential crossing points of the Colorado and

that Link J22, on route 894 was the place which best meets all Commission criteria for such a

crossing. The recommendation of Route 894 by both the Applicant and the Judges was thus

based on a comprehensive analysis of the applicable criteria, using actual data when it was

available.


          In contrast, the selection of Route 487 as the preferred route by PUC Staff was not

conducted using any weighting criteria or other data analysis. Route 487 selected by PUC

Staff only has the appearance of standing out when compared to the extremes of the other

routes in the Environmental Assessment. Staff actually claims in its Exceptions that the

PFD “gives undue weight to Route 894' s 1-mile distance from Colorado Bend State Park

as a distinguishing factor to recommend the selection of Route 894 over Route 487.” 3.

There are multiple problems with this statement.

          First, on cross – examination PUC witness Poole confirmed that link J11 crosses

within 100 feet of the entrance to Colorado Bend State Park. 4 This is obviously not the

“1-mile distance” stated in Staff’s Exceptions and is a mis- statement of the actual

evidence. He also confirmed that this was a “problem “with his original




2
    Direct Testimony of Casey Petty at 13-14.
3 Staff Exceptions at 14.
4 See also Poole Direct Testimony at 40.

                                                     3
 recommendation. He additionally admitted that there are good reasons to cross where

there is already an existing transmission line crossing.

        Second, a preponderance of intervenor witnesses who provided testimony on this subject

opposed the Route 487 crossing point of the Colorado (using Link J11). Some examples follow:


        Dr. Andrew Sansom for Wullf Bluff Creek Ranch also supported using different links

from J11 to cross the Colorado. Sansom conducts a careful analysis of the potential crossing

points. “Based on my review of materials in the Application, the central crossing locations

involving Links U2 and Jll are among those most proximate to Colorado Bend State Park and

other notable natural features along the river corridor. The proximity of those crossings to highly

valued recreational and natural areas warrants careful consideration of potential visual,

environmental, and long-term corridor impacts.” He ultimately recommends Link U3. 5


        “Link U3 crosses the Colorado River in a location that parallels existing electric

transmission infrastructure, whereas every other link that crosses the Colorado River would

create a new crossing corridor. By utilizing Link U3, the proposed transmission line would

consolidate infrastructure within an existing corridor rather than introducing a whole new

crossing location.” 6


        “If the Commission finds that the Applicants have presented a route or routes that meet

the statutory and regulatory standards, the Commission should avoid approving a crossing of

the Colorado River at a previously undisturbed area.” 7




5 Direct Testimony of Andrew H. Sansom at 8-13.
6 Direct Testimony of Dr. Joshua Rhodes on behalf of Solana Ranch, et.al. at 13. emph. supp.
7 Direct Testimony of Barry T. Smitherman on behalf of Save the Lampasas et.al at 21. emph. supp.

                                                       4
        Cherokee Creek witness Reinecke notes that J11 is one of the links which crosses the

Colorado at a TPWD designated Ecologically Significant Stream Segment.


       “Q: WHY IS THE COLORADO RIVER CROSSING IMPORTANT TO YOUR

ANALYSIS?


       A: The Colorado River serves as major a hydrologic and biological corridor through the

broader region. Portions of the river provide USFWS-designated critical habitat for species listed

and proposed under the ESA and are recognized by TPWD as ESSS. Thus, the Colorado River

crossing should not be evaluated merely as one additional stream crossing in a numerical count.

A crossing of the Colorado River may affect not only the river channel itself, but also the

associated riparian corridor, adjacent woodland, wildlife movement, scenic quality, and

recreational experience in the surrounding area. Given the overall project alignment, all route

alternatives must cross the feature at some point. So, given that it cannot be avoided, I evaluated

the location and context of the proposed link crossings to see if there were opportunities to

minimize potential impact.


       Q: WHERE IS THE PORTION OF THE COLORADO RIVER WITHIN THE STUDY

AREA DESIGNATED AS AN ESSS?


       A: The ESSS-designated segment extends from where the Colorado River enters the

northern edge of the Study Area downstream to its confluence with Yancey Creek, just north of

the 22 Lampasas/Burnet County line. As reflected in Table RLSR-7, Links U3, U2, and Jll cross

the designated ESSS portion of the Colorado River. These are the three northernmost proposed

crossings of the river within the Study Area.


                                                 5
         Q: DID YOU NOTICE ANY ADDITIONAL DIFFERENCES AMONG THE

PROPOSED COLORADO RIVER CROSSINGS?


        A: Yes. I observed two notable distinctions. First, the Colorado River crossings

associated with Links Jll, J22, and J26 are located in relatively close proximity to Colorado

Bend State Park and/or Post Oak Ridge State Park. That proximity may compound the potential

impacts of a transmission line crossing because it combines major river crossing impacts with

potential visual, scenic, and recreational effects on nearby public park resources.” She then

recommends Link J31. 8


        Hodge and Schwertner’s witness Brian Andrews also supports avoidance of the Link J11

area.


        “Q ARE THERE UNIQUE CIRCUMSTANCES IN THIS PROCEEDING?


        A. Yes. All 122 filed alternative routes must cross the Colorado River to connect the Bell

County East Switch with the Big Hill Substation in Schleicher County. Colorado Bend State

Park (approximately 5,300 acres) and Post Oak Ridge State Park (approximately 7 3,170 acres)

lie along the Colorado River in the central portion of the study area, occupying approximately

8,500 acres collectively. Post Oak Ridge State Park was one of the first three parks acquired

using the voter-approved $1 billion Centennial Parks Conservation Fund, underscoring the public

significance of this resource. Because the location of each Colorado River crossing relative to

these two state parks varies across the filed routes, the visual impact analysis presented in

Section 7.7 of the Environmental Assessment is an important consideration in this proceeding.



8 Direct Testimony of Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke on behalf of Segment K13/K51 Landowners at 42-43.

                                                   6
 The Application includes multiple routes that avoid foreground visual impacts on these state

parks with otherwise comparable routing-factor performance and only modest estimated cost

differences.


        Q WHICH LINKS PASS WITHIN THE FOREGROUND VISUAL ZONE OF THE

STATE PARKS, AND WHICH ROUTES DO NOT USE THOSE LINKS?


        A. Two links pass within the half-mile foreground visual zone of one or both of the

state parks in the study area: Link Jll and Link J26. Across the 122 filed routes, ROW within

the foreground visual zone of state parks and recreational areas ranges from 0.00 miles to 8.68

miles. Per Section 7.7.5 of the Environmental Assessment, Link Jll is approximately 100 feet

from the northern boundary of Colorado Bend State Park and spans Colorado Park Road, the

park's primary entrance road. The park's main entrance and fee booth, approximately 1.5 miles

of the Tie Slide Trail, the River Overlook, and approximately one mile of the Gorman Falls

Trail are within the half-mile foreground visual zone of Link J11. Twenty-five of the 122 filed

routes use Link J11.” Andrews ultimately recommended Route 894. 9


        Staff has thus not only mis-characterized the actual distance and proximity to the

proposed route but also ignored the previously undisturbed character of the proposed Colorado

crossing, the ESSS designation of the river at that point, and the foreground visual impacts of

that crossing. The deficiencies of Route 487 as to environmental integrity and effects on parks

and recreational areas is made obvious here.




9 Direct Testimony of Brian C. Andrews on behalf of Hodge and Schwertner parties at 13-14.

                                                     7
          The additional reasoning Staff provided in its Exceptions (at 16-20) is also not

persuasive, as in other respects Route 487 is not shown to be substantially superior to Route 894,

as to length, cost or number of habitable structures as shown in the Applicant Testimony

referenced above.


         J27 Landowners actually appear to oppose both Route 894 and Route 487. 10 Their

reasoning for preferring 487 over 894 if that is the only choice fails for the same reasons argued

above.


                                               Conclusion


         The Commission should reject Route 487 or any route that includes Link J11, as it would

unnecessarily impact a single, contiguous, and interconnected landscape and the surrounding

ranchlands. Together, these areas form one of the most intact, unspoiled, and carefully preserved

landscapes in Central Texas.


         The effects of Link J11 would extend well beyond any single property. It would fragment

an otherwise cohesive ecological corridor, degrade a landscape of recognized historical and

cultural significance, needlessly create a new and unsightly crossing of the Colorado River and

adversely affect the broader community that depends on these resources for identity, recreation,

and economic activity. These impacts would not be isolated or temporary, but structural and

enduring.


         Instead, the Commission should select a route that minimizes environmental impact,

avoids fragmentation of intact ranchland and wildlife habitat, and preserves the integrity of this


10 J27 Landowner Exceptions at 6-7.

                                                  8
 landscape, including unnecessary new and intrusive crossings of the Colorado River. That

includes protecting not only individual features, but the continuity, context, and views that give

this area its significance.


        WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDEDRED, Lampasas J11 Landowners respectfully

request that Staff’s preferred Route 487, including Link J11, no longer be considered as any part

of the route to be considered for any transmission line, as it will have such a devastating and

detrimental impact on its property, as well as the crossing of an untouched pristine area of the

Colorado River. We further recommend Route 894, and would not oppose Routes 296, 392,

410,572, 891 and CCG in addition to Route 894 to be selected and for such further and other

relief as may be granted.


                                               Respectively submitted,


                                               _/s/Roger B. Borgelt _

in accordance with the rules set forth in the SOAH Order.
